idiom_name: constructor or setter injection (Spring/CDI) plus explicit method parameters
implementation_notes: Java's classic relay is the method or constructor parameter carried through layers that do not use it - JEP 506's motivation describes exactly that: a method may have to include in its parameter list things its indirect callee needs even though it does not use them itself. The mainstream answer is to inject the dependency where it is used (constructor injection with Spring/CDI, or plain factories at the composition root) so intermediates never see it. Explicit parameters remain right for values the class actually uses and for signatures that should stay self-documenting.
pitfalls: A container that injects ten collaborators into one class recreates the relay at class level instead of method level, and hides the dependency graph behind annotations.
Field injection (`@Autowired` on a field) defeats the constructor signature and makes the class untestable without a container.

variants.name: Scoped values (JDK 25) for immutable per-request data
variants.implementation_notes: Java 25 finalised scoped values (JEP 506, after previews in JDK 21-24). A `ScopedValue` is a static final key that a caller binds for a bounded dynamic scope; callees at any depth read it with `KEY.get()` without the value appearing in their signatures, and child threads started inside the scope inherit the binding. That replaces `ThreadLocal` for per-request data - immutable, no leak on thread reuse, cheaper with virtual threads - while keeping the binding's lifetime visible in the syntactic structure. Prefer it over parameter threading only when the value is genuinely wide and immutable.
pitfalls: ScopedValue bindings are immutable and only visible inside the run/call scope, so mutable request state still needs an explicit parameter or a request object.
`ThreadLocal` remains in the language and still leaks on pooled or virtual threads unless removed in a `finally` block - do not mix the two idioms for the same value.
